about: Hand-written columns. The builder folds them into public/questions/nfl.json. Each clue: clue, answer, wrong (3 or more wrong answers), level (1 easy to 5 hard), and optionally also (other answers that count).

categories.title: Legends & Lore
categories.description: The coaches, stars, nicknames and traditions that built the NFL.

clues.clue: The Super Bowl trophy carries the name of this coach, who won the first two Super Bowls with Green Bay.
Going 17-0 in 1972, this team finished the only unbeaten, untied season capped by a Super Bowl title.
Three days before Super Bowl III, this Jets quarterback guaranteed a win over the heavily favored Colts, then delivered it.
This Browns running back led the NFL in rushing in 8 of his 9 seasons, then retired at 30 to make movies.
Nicknamed Sweetness, this Bears running back retired in 1987 as the NFL's career rushing leader.
Pittsburgh's 1970s defense, led by Joe Greene and Jack Lambert, went by this nickname.
Alan Page, Carl Eller, Jim Marshall and Gary Larsen made up this Minnesota defensive line.
Deacon Jones, Merlin Olsen, Lamar Lundy and Rosey Grier formed this Los Angeles Rams front four.
Denver's late-1970s defense, which carried the Broncos to Super Bowl XII, was nicknamed this.
Bob Lilly, Randy White and Too Tall Jones played for this Dallas defense, named for the end of the world.
Tom Landry said he couldn't recall the names of the 1972 Dolphins defenders, giving them this nickname.
Miami's early-1980s defense earned this nickname because so many starters' last names began with B.
Washington's offensive line of the 1980s, with Russ Grimm and Joe Jacoby, was known by this barnyard nickname.
Buffalo's offensive line was nicknamed this because it turned on the Juice, O.J. Simpson.
This Rams defensive end is credited with coining the word sack for tackling a quarterback.
From 1956 to 1960 this Colts quarterback threw a touchdown pass in 47 straight games, a record for 52 years.
As a rookie in 1965, the Kansas Comet scored 6 touchdowns in one game for the Bears.
The award for college football's best linebacker is named for this ferocious Bears linebacker of 1965 to 1973.
The Galloping Ghost signed with the Bears in 1925 and drew huge crowds on a barnstorming tour.
An Olympic champion in 1912, he was named the first president of the league that became the NFL.
The NFL was founded in this Ohio city in 1920, and the Pro Football Hall of Fame sits there today.
The NFL played its first two seasons under this name before changing it in 1922.
Papa Bear founded the Decatur Staleys in 1920 and coached the Bears for 40 seasons.
He founded the Packers in 1919, and their stadium now bears his name.
Cleveland's team was named after this coach, who later founded the Cincinnati Bengals in 1968.
Wearing his trademark fedora, he coached the Dallas Cowboys for their first 29 seasons.
With the Colts and Dolphins, he won 347 games, the most by any head coach.
This coach won four Super Bowls with the Steelers in the six seasons from 1974 to 1979.
Wired for sound in Super Bowl IV, this Chiefs coach was heard calling for the 65 toss power trap.
This stoic Vikings coach took Minnesota to four Super Bowls and lost them all.
This Packers quarterback was named MVP of the first two Super Bowls.
This Chiefs quarterback was MVP of Super Bowl IV, a 23-7 win over Minnesota.
This AFL founder and Chiefs owner came up with the name Super Bowl, inspired by his children's toy ball.
Commissioner from 1960 to 1989, he now has his name on the Super Bowl MVP trophy.
In 1971 this Vikings defensive tackle became the first defensive player named the league's MVP.
Mean Joe tossed his jersey to a young fan in a famous 1979 Coca-Cola commercial.
In 1973 this Bills running back became the first to run for 2,000 yards in a season, and he did it in 14 games.
In 1984 this Rams running back set the single-season rushing record with 2,105 yards.
Night Train intercepted 14 passes as a rookie in 1952, a record that still stands.
The Golden Boy scored 176 points for the Packers in 1960, in a season of only 12 games.
This Packers receiver of 1935 to 1945 retired with 99 touchdown catches, a record for over 40 years.
In 1943 Slingin' Sammy led the league in passing, punting and interceptions for Washington.
This Browns quarterback played in a league championship game in all 10 of his seasons and won 7 of them.
Concrete Charlie, the last full-time two-way player, flattened Frank Gifford with a famous 1960 hit.
This Giants star of the 1950s later spent decades calling Monday Night Football.
Calling Monday Night Football, this broadcaster made He could go all the way! a catchphrase.
Before he was a broadcaster and video game name, he coached the Raiders to a Super Bowl XI win.
The Snake was the left-handed quarterback of the 1970s Raiders.
This scrambling quarterback retired in 1978 holding the career records for passing yards and touchdowns.
A Heisman winner at Navy, this Cowboys quarterback served in Vietnam before starting his NFL career.
This quarterback won four Super Bowls with Pittsburgh in the 1970s.
His leaping, juggling catches made this Steelers receiver the MVP of Super Bowl X.
This Dolphins fullback ran over Minnesota for MVP honors in Super Bowl VIII.
The AFL and NFL agreed to merge in 1966, and they became one league in this year.
The first Super Bowl, in January 1967, was played in this Los Angeles stadium.
This coach won the 1958 NFL title with the Colts and Super Bowl III with the Jets.
Born without toes on his kicking foot, he booted a record 63-yard field goal for the Saints in 1970.
This quarterback and kicker played 26 seasons and didn't retire until he was 48.
In 1964 this Vikings defensive end scooped up a fumble and ran 66 yards the wrong way for a safety.
In 1946 he and Woody Strode signed with the Los Angeles Rams, reintegrating the NFL.
In 1921 he became the NFL's first Black head coach, sharing the job with the Akron Pros.
In 1989 the Raiders made this Hall of Fame tackle the first Black head coach of the modern era.
In Super Bowl XXII he became the first Black quarterback to start and win a Super Bowl, throwing 4 touchdowns in one quarter.
Mr. Cowboy was the first draft pick in Dallas Cowboys history, in 1961.
This 49ers coach built the West Coast offense and won three Super Bowls in the 1980s.
This 49ers quarterback won four Super Bowls without throwing an interception in any of them.
In 1986 this Giants linebacker became only the second defensive player named league MVP.
The Fridge, a 300-pound defensive tackle, scored a touchdown for the Bears in Super Bowl XX.
This Bears defensive end, the 46 defense's sack leader, was MVP of Super Bowl XX.
The Chicago Bears have long been known by this nickname, from the city's Midway Plaisance.
Just win, baby was the motto of this longtime Raiders owner.
He caught passes on the 1963 champion Bears and coached them to a Super Bowl XX title.
This Washington coach won three Super Bowls with three different starting quarterbacks.
Don Coryell's pass-happy San Diego offense of the late 1970s and 1980s was called this.
Jim Kelly ran this no-huddle attack for the Buffalo Bills of the early 1990s.
Warren Moon threw out of this four-receiver offense for the Houston Oilers.
Kurt Warner, Marshall Faulk and the Rams of 1999 to 2001 were called this.
Richard Sherman, Earl Thomas and Kam Chancellor patrolled this Seattle secondary.
This Bengals rookie running back's touchdown dance, the Shuffle, swept the nation in 1988.
This Packers safety made the first Lambeau Leap into the stands, in 1993.
Giants players started the Gatorade bath tradition by dousing this head coach in the 1980s.
This Steelers broadcaster created the Terrible Towel in 1975.
The barking fans in the end zone seats of this team's stadium are the Dawg Pound.
In 1984 this team retired the number 12 in honor of its fans, the 12th Man.
This team has played at home on Thanksgiving Day every year since 1934, apart from the war years.
For most of the years from 1980 to 2016, the Pro Bowl was played in this city.
The NFL's official game ball, The Duke, is named for this longtime Giants owner.
In 1976 this former player started the tradition of honoring the last pick of the draft as Mr. Irrelevant.
College football had it for decades, but the NFL didn't add the two-point conversion until this year.
Playing for San Francisco and Oakland, he retired with career records for catches, receiving yards and touchdowns.
Mostly with Buffalo, this defensive end piled up 200 sacks, the official career record.
Playing safety for Washington and Minnesota, he intercepted 81 passes, the career record.
In 2001 this Giants defensive end set a new single-season sack record with 22.5.
In 2013 he set single-season records for Denver with 5,477 passing yards and 55 touchdown passes.
In 2006 this Chargers running back scored a then-record 31 touchdowns.
In 2007 he caught a record 23 touchdown passes from Tom Brady.
Megatron set the single-season receiving record with 1,964 yards in 2012.
In 1984 this Dolphins quarterback became the first to throw for 5,000 yards in a season.
This Cowboys running back retired with 18,355 rushing yards, the career record.
This Packers quarterback started 297 straight regular-season games.
This kicker retired with 2,673 points, the most in NFL history, and four Super Bowl rings.
In 1999 this Lions running back faxed his retirement to a newspaper, about 1,500 yards short of the career rushing record.
Prime Time is the only man to play in both a World Series and a Super Bowl.
This Raiders running back was also a Kansas City Royals outfielder, an All-Star in both sports.

categories.title: Greatest Hits
categories.description: The plays and games with names of their own.

clues.clue: Franco Harris caught a deflected pass at his shoetops and ran it in to beat Oakland in this 1972 play.
He scooped up the Immaculate Reception and ran it in for Pittsburgh.
The Steelers beat this team on the Immaculate Reception.
The Immaculate Reception bounced off Frenchy Fuqua or this hard-hitting Raiders defensive back, or both.
Joe Montana's leaping touchdown to Dwight Clark beat Dallas for the 1981 NFC title in this play.
Leaping in the back of the end zone, he made The Catch for San Francisco.
The Catch sent San Francisco to its first Super Bowl at the expense of this team.
In a January 1999 playoff game, Steve Young hit this receiver with 3 seconds left to beat Green Bay in The Catch II.
John Elway's 98-yard march to tie the 1986 AFC title game in Cleveland is remembered as this.
John Elway led The Drive in the AFC title game to beat this team in overtime.
The Drive covered this many yards, from the shadow of Denver's own goal line.
A year after The Drive, this Browns running back was stripped near the goal line in Denver, a play known as The Fumble.
In 1978 Ken Stabler fumbled forward, and the Raiders batted the ball into the end zone to beat San Diego in this play.
This Raiders tight end finished the Holy Roller by falling on the ball in the end zone.
The Holy Roller beat this team, and the league changed its fumble rules afterward.
The 1967 NFL title game at Lambeau Field, played at about 13 below zero, is known as this.
Green Bay beat this team in the Ice Bowl on Bart Starr's quarterback sneak.
This Packers guard threw the block that let Bart Starr sneak in to win the Ice Bowl.
In 1968 NBC cut away from a Jets-Raiders game for a children's movie and missed two late Oakland touchdowns, giving the game this name.
The 1958 NFL title game, won by Baltimore in sudden-death overtime at Yankee Stadium, earned this nickname.
This Colts fullback plunged in from a yard out to win the 1958 title game in overtime.
Johnny Unitas and this team beat the New York Giants in the 1958 title game.
Clarence Davis grabbed a game-winning touchdown among several Miami defenders in this 1974 playoff play.
Ken Stabler's long pass to tight end Dave Casper set up the tying kick in a 1977 double-overtime playoff win at Baltimore, a play called this.
San Diego's 41-38 overtime playoff win in Miami in January 1982 is remembered as this.
This Chargers tight end caught 13 passes and blocked a field goal in the Epic in Miami, then had to be helped off the field.
With a wind chill near 59 below, the 1981 AFC title game in Cincinnati got this name.
This team won the Freezer Bowl to reach its first Super Bowl.
Roger Staubach threw the original Hail Mary in a 1975 playoff game, to this receiver.
Dallas beat this team on Roger Staubach's 1975 Hail Mary.
In January 1993 this backup quarterback rallied Buffalo from 35-3 down to beat Houston in overtime.
Buffalo's comeback from 35-3 down in January 1993 came against this team.
Buffalo's 1993 playoff win over Houston, known as The Comeback, erased a deficit of this many points.
Frank Wycheck's lateral and Kevin Dyson's kickoff return beat Buffalo in this January 2000 play.
He took the lateral and ran 75 yards for the Titans in the Music City Miracle.
This Titans tight end threw the cross-field lateral in the Music City Miracle.
The Music City Miracle knocked this team out of the playoffs.
This Rams linebacker stopped Kevin Dyson a yard short on the last play of Super Bowl XXXIV.
Mike Jones's game-saving stop on the final play of Super Bowl XXXIV is known simply as this.
His 47-yard kick sailed wide right on the last play of Super Bowl XXV.
This team won Super Bowl XXV 20-19 when Buffalo's last kick went wide right.
In a snowy January 2002 playoff game, an apparent Tom Brady fumble against Oakland was overturned under this rule.
This Raiders cornerback hit Tom Brady on the Tuck Rule play, a sack that was reversed.
He pinned a pass against his helmet to keep the Giants' winning drive alive in Super Bowl XLII.
David Tyree's grab against his headgear in Super Bowl XLII is called this.
On Thanksgiving 2012, this Jets quarterback ran into a teammate's backside and fumbled in the Butt Fumble.
Mark Sanchez ran into the backside of this Jets guard on the Butt Fumble.
The Butt Fumble came in a 49-19 Thanksgiving loss to this team.
Nick Foles caught a touchdown pass on a 4th-and-goal trick play in Super Bowl LII, a play known as this.
This Eagles tight end threw the touchdown pass to Nick Foles on the Philly Special.
On the Philly Special, this Eagles quarterback slipped out and caught the touchdown himself.
With 10 seconds left in a January 2018 playoff game, Stefon Diggs caught a pass and ran 61 yards to beat New Orleans in this play.
This Vikings receiver ran untouched into the end zone in the Minneapolis Miracle.
This quarterback threw the Minneapolis Miracle pass.
This undrafted rookie jumped a goal-line pass to win Super Bowl XLIX for New England.
Malcolm Butler's Super Bowl XLIX interception was thrown by this quarterback.
Malcolm Butler cut in front of this Seahawks receiver for the Super Bowl XLIX interception.
His 67-yard tackle-breaking touchdown run against New Orleans in January 2011 set off the Beast Quake.
Seattle fans jumped so hard on Marshawn Lynch's 67-yard run that a seismograph picked it up, giving the play this name.
Replacement officials gave this Seahawks receiver a disputed last-play touchdown against Green Bay in the 2012 Fail Mary.
The disputed last-second Seahawks win over Green Bay in 2012, called by replacement officials, got this nickname.
His last-second kick hit the upright and the crossbar in the Double Doink that ended the Bears' 2018 season.
In October 2000 the Jets came back from 30-7 down in the fourth quarter to beat Miami 40-37 in overtime, a game called this.
This Jets quarterback threw five touchdown passes in the Monday Night Miracle.
In 2003 the Saints scored on a last-play pass with three laterals in Jacksonville, then missed the extra point, a play called this.
This veteran Saints kicker pushed the extra point wide after the River City Relay.
In 1978, instead of kneeling, the Giants handed off and fumbled, and this Eagles cornerback ran it back to win the Miracle at the Meadowlands.
In 2010 his walk-off punt return finished Philadelphia's comeback in the Miracle at the New Meadowlands.
In January 2022 Kansas City needed just this many seconds to tie Buffalo at the end of regulation, then won in overtime.
In 1982 a man on a snowplow cleared a spot for a Patriots kick to beat Miami 3-0, in a game known as this.
The Snowplow Game left this team angry about a 3-0 loss in Foxborough.
A thick fog rolled over Soldier Field during a Bears playoff win over the Eagles on New Year's Eve 1988, a game known as this.
With 31 seconds left in a January 2013 playoff game in Denver, Joe Flacco hit this receiver for a 70-yard tying touchdown.
Joe Flacco's 70-yard bomb to tie Denver in the closing seconds of a January 2013 playoff game is called this.
A day after his father died in December 2003, this quarterback threw for 399 yards and 4 touchdowns on Monday Night Football in Oakland.
Showboating on a fumble return in Super Bowl XXVII, he was stripped just short of the goal line by Don Beebe.
This Bills receiver chased down Leon Lett and knocked the ball loose at the goal line in Super Bowl XXVII.
In Super Bowl VII, this Dolphins kicker had a field goal blocked, tried to throw a pass, and watched it returned for a touchdown.
A Hall of Fame tight end, he dropped a wide-open touchdown pass for Dallas in Super Bowl XIII.
His toe-tapping catch in the corner of the end zone with 35 seconds left won Super Bowl XLIII for Pittsburgh.
At the end of the first half of Super Bowl XLIII, this Steelers linebacker returned an interception 100 yards for a touchdown.
He caught a deflected pass inches off the turf, among three defenders, during the Patriots' Super Bowl LI comeback.
New England came back from 28-3 down to beat this team in Super Bowl LI.
On Sunday Night Football in 2014 this Giants rookie made a one-handed touchdown catch against Dallas while being interfered with.
On Monday Night Football in 2000, this Packers receiver caught a deflected pass while lying on his back to beat Minnesota in overtime.
On New Year's Day 2006 this 43-year-old Patriots backup made the NFL's first successful drop kick since 1941.
This Raiders running back reversed field for a 74-yard touchdown in a Super Bowl XVIII rout of Washington.
This Packers returner took a kickoff 99 yards for a touchdown and won MVP of Super Bowl XXXI.
Super Bowl XLVII was stopped for over half an hour when the power went out in this stadium.
This Saints cornerback sealed Super Bowl XLIV with a 74-yard interception return off Peyton Manning.
This Saints coach opened the second half of Super Bowl XLIV with a surprise onside kick called Ambush.
Kyler Murray heaved a 43-yard Hail Murray to this receiver, who caught it among three Bills to win in 2020.
